question: How do I price an add-on SKU when my base product is underpriced?
answer:
Don't raise base pricing and bundle an add-on; instead, create a *separate* tier where the add-on is the anchor. If your base is $500/month, add-on is $250/month standalone. Offer a "combo" at $650 (list it as $500 + $250 = $750, discount to $650). Now the add-on has perceived value without devaluing your base. Price anchoring psychology: bundle upward, not sideways. Your base stays the same; your revenue grows. ## Add-On Pricing Strategy 1. **Separate value communication.** Your base solves Problem A (40% of their pain). The add-on solves Problem B (an adjacent, 30% pain point). If customers are buying base + add-on, price them separately so the combo looks like a bargain. "[Feature] is normally $250/month—we've bundled it at $150 for annual subscribers." The $100 discount feels real. 2. **Use a multi-tier architecture.** - **Tier 1 (Base):** $500/month—solves core problem - **Tier 2 (Base + Add-on 1):** $650/month—adds workflow automation - **Tier 3 (Base + Add-ons 1 & 2):** $900/month—enterprise reporting This creates clear upgrade paths. You're not forcing people to buy add-ons; you're showing them that *stacking* value is cheaper than buying separately. 3. **Price add-ons at 25–40% of base, not 10%.** If your base is $500, an add-on priced at $50 looks like a throwaway feature. Price it at $125–$200 (it *is* real value), then discount it in a bundle. This signals that you're confident in what it does. 4. **Use annual discounts to compress margin pressure.** If a customer wants month-to-month base + add-on at discount rates, require annual commitment on the bundle. "Annual bundled plan is $650/month. Month-to-month is $700." The $50/month incentive drives commitment without looking desperate. ## The Underpriced Base Trap If your base is underpriced (you know it is), raising it *later* costs you churn and friction. Instead, create new value above it. The add-on isn't about "getting more from existing customers." It's about building a value ladder. Customers who graduate from base to base + add-on are the ones most likely to stay long-term because they've invested in your entire product, not just one piece. **Benchmark:** SaaS products with 3+ tiers have 2.3× higher NRR than those with single pricing (OpenView). More tiers = more customer segments finding a fit. Trap: Treating add-ons as "nice-to-have" features. Instead, position them as "most customers eventually adopt this."
